# Exploratory data analysis {#sec-exploratory}

Before any model, look at the data. Exploration has four jobs [@zuur2010protocol]: find
**errors and outliers**, understand the **structure** of the data — what counts as a
replicate —, see the **distributions** that models will have to describe, and detect
**collinearity** between variables that a model will struggle to separate. Skipping it
does not save time: the problems are still there, and they surface later as strange
model results.

The simulated ponds of the previous chapters are too clean for this. This chapter uses
real data, with all the problems real data have.

::: {.callout-note}
## Where this chapter comes from

Like @sec-own-functions and @sec-resampling, this chapter is **inspired by** **ecoR**
[@oliveira_ecor], the R course wiki of the Instituto de Biociências, Universidade de
São Paulo, produced and maintained by Alexandre Adalardo de Oliveira. Its sequence —
checking the data frame, descriptive statistics, univariate graphs, relationships
between variables, and the Anscombe quartet — follows ecoR's exploratory-analysis
module. The text, data, examples and exercises here are written from scratch for Julia;
the authors of ecoR have not reviewed this book.

If you read Portuguese and want to go further, the original material is freely
available (CC BY-SA 4.0):

- [4. Análise Exploratória de Dados](https://ecor.ib.usp.br/doku.php?id=03_apostila:05-exploratoria)
  — the course notes;
- [4. Tutoriais de Análise Exploratória de Dados](https://ecor.ib.usp.br/doku.php?id=02_tutoriais:tutorial4:start)
  — the step-by-step tutorial;
- [exercises on exploratory analysis](https://ecor.ib.usp.br/doku.php?id=01_curso_atual:exercicios4),
  automatically graded in [notaR](http://notar.ib.usp.br), in R.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## The data: ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS

**ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS** [@rodrigues2019atlantic] compiles morphological measurements
of birds from the Atlantic forests of South America: 72 483 records, gathered from
museum collections, ringing projects and the literature between 1820 and 2018, by 179
authors. Its data paper states that there are no copyright or proprietary restrictions
on its use, and asks that it be cited when used in publications or teaching — as here.

`data/atlantic_bird_traits.csv` keeps **all** records and 21 of the original 83
columns, with their original names and codes. Nothing is cleaned: finding the problems
is the point. `scripts/prepare_birds.jl` documents how the subset was made from the
original file, which is in the paper's supporting information.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: setup-07
using TidierData
using DataFrames, CSV
using Statistics, StatsBase
using GLM, RDatasets, Distributions
using CairoMakie

CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png")
bird_file = joinpath("..", "data", "atlantic_bird_traits.csv")
```

```{julia}
#| label: checker-07
#| include: false
include(joinpath("..", "exercises", "check.jl"))
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Exercises in this chapter

The answers are numbers computed from the bird data. Start each session with:

```julia
include("exercises/check.jl")
using TidierData, DataFrames, CSV, Statistics, StatsBase, GLM, Distributions
bird_file = joinpath("data", "atlantic_bird_traits.csv")
```

The first section shows how to read the file; the later exercises assume you have read
it that way, into `birds`, with the columns renamed.
:::

## First contact: reading the file {#sec-eda-read}

Read the file as it comes and look at the type of each column:

```{julia}
#| label: read-naive
raw = CSV.read(bird_file, DataFrame)
size(raw)
```

```{julia}
#| label: types-naive
first(describe(raw, :eltype, :nmissing), 8)
```

Body mass, wing length, tail length: all read as **text** (`String`), and not one value
is missing. The reason is in the file itself — missing values are written as the two
letters `NA`, which `CSV.jl` does not treat as missing by default. One non-number in a
column makes the whole column text. Tell `CSV.read` which code means missing:

```{julia}
#| label: read-na
birds = CSV.read(bird_file, DataFrame; missingstring = "NA")
first(describe(birds, :eltype, :nmissing), 8)
```

::: {.r-equivalent}
**In R**

`read.csv` treats `"NA"` as missing by default, so in R this problem would pass
unnoticed. Here it is visible: a numeric column that arrives as text is the first sign
that the file uses a missing-value code you have not declared. Other common codes are
`""`, `"-"`, `"."`, `-999` and `99999`; `missingstring` also accepts a vector of them.
:::

The column names mix units, dots and capitals, like `Body_mass.g.`. They are awkward to
type and Tidier macros cannot use them directly. Rename them once, at the start:

```{julia}
#| label: rename
rename!(birds,
    "ID_ABT" => :id, "Order" => :order, "Family" => :family, "Binomial" => :species,
    "Body_mass.g." => :mass_g, "Wing_length.mm." => :wing_mm,
    "Tail_length.mm." => :tail_mm, "Tarsus_length.mm." => :tarsus_mm,
    "Bill_length.mm." => :bill_mm, "Age" => :age, "Sex" => :sex, "Status" => :status,
    "Recapture" => :recapture, "Ring" => :ring,
    "Latitude_decimal_degrees" => :lat, "Longitude_decimal_degrees" => :lon,
    "Altitude" => :altitude, "Year" => :year, "Main_researcher" => :source,
    "Outside.range" => :outside_range, "Obs.spp" => :species_note)

names(birds)
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 7.1 — How many birds were weighed?

How many records have a body mass? Pass the number to `check("7.1", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

`count(!ismissing, v)` counts the non-missing values of a vector. It only means
something once the file has been read with `missingstring = "NA"`.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-7-1
n_mass = count(!ismissing, birds.mass_g)
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-7-1-check
check("7.1", n_mass)
```

60 819 of 72 483: body mass is the most commonly recorded trait, and still missing for
one record in six.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-7-1
#| include: false
Checks.verify("7.1", n_mass)
```

## Missing, unknown, and inconsistent {#sec-eda-codes}

Categorical columns deserve a table of their levels before anything else:

```{julia}
#| label: levels-age-sex
(age = countmap(birds.age), sex = countmap(birds.sex))
```

There are **two kinds of missing** here. `missing` means the information was never
recorded; `"Unknown"` means someone looked at the bird and could not tell. They are not
the same thing: a study of sex ratios should count the unknowns, but not the unrecorded.

Other columns disagree with themselves about spelling:

```{julia}
#| label: levels-case
(recapture = countmap(birds.recapture), outside_range = countmap(birds.outside_range))
```

`"no"` and `"Yes"`: the capitalization differs between levels. Here it is harmless,
because each level has only one spelling, but a single `"yes"` somewhere would create a
third level that grouping would treat as different. Normalizing is cheap:

```{julia}
#| label: normalize
birds.recapture     = passmissing(lowercase).(birds.recapture)
birds.outside_range = lowercase.(birds.outside_range)
unique(birds.recapture)
```

`passmissing(f)` applies `f` to values and leaves `missing` alone.

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 7.2 — How often can sex be told?

Among records where sex was **recorded** (not `missing`), what proportion were sexed as
`"Male"` or `"Female"`? Pass it to `check("7.2", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Keep the non-missing values with `collect(skipmissing(birds.sex))`, then take the mean
of `in(("Male", "Female")).(...)`.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-7-2
sex_recorded = collect(skipmissing(birds.sex))
p_sexed = mean(in(("Male", "Female")).(sex_recorded))
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-7-2-check
check("7.2", p_sexed)
```

Less than half: many Atlantic forest passerines cannot be sexed in the hand. Any
analysis by sex is an analysis of a non-random half of the data.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-7-2
#| include: false
Checks.verify("7.2", p_sexed)
```

## Structure: what is a replicate? {#sec-eda-structure}

A row is a record, but records are not independent observations. They are grouped in
several ways at once.

**By species.** The records are very unequally spread:

```{julia}
#| label: per-species
per_species = sort(combine(groupby(birds, :species), nrow => :n), :n, rev = true)

(names = nrow(per_species),
 top_five = first(per_species, 5),
 with_one_record = count(==(1), per_species.n))
```

780 names — some identified only to genus, such as `Elaenia sp.` — while the data paper
reports 711 species. Before counting species, decide what counts as one. The ten most
recorded species hold a fifth of all records; 68 names appear once.

**By individual.** A ringed bird caught again appears again:

```{julia}
#| label: rings
ringed = dropmissing(birds[:, [:ring, :species]], :ring)
per_ring = combine(groupby(ringed, :ring), :species => (s -> length(unique(s))) => :n_species,
                   nrow => :n)
first(sort(per_ring[per_ring.n_species .> 1, :], :n, rev = true), 6)
```

Some "rings" are shared by more than twenty species. They are not ring numbers but
**colour-band codes** such as `BRD` or `BLUE RIGHT`, which many birds carry. A naive
count of recaptures would take all those birds for one individual.

**By source and method.** Each record comes from one of 65 main researchers, and from
live birds or museum skins, over two centuries:

```{julia}
#| label: status-year
combine(groupby(dropmissing(birds[:, [:status, :year]]), :status),
        nrow => :n, :year => minimum => :first, :year => median => :median,
        :year => maximum => :last)
```

Each of these groupings can make records from the same group more alike than records
from different groups — the dependence that the mixed models of @sec-mixed-models
account for. Exploring the structure tells you which grouping terms a model needs.

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 7.3 — How many birds were caught twice?

Count the individuals recorded more than once: rings that appear in more than one
record **of the same species**, ignoring ring codes made only of letters (colour-band
codes). Pass the number to `check("7.3", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Drop the letter-only codes with `occursin(r"^[A-Za-z]+$", ring)`, which is `true` for
them. Then group by `ring` **and** `species`, count rows, and count the groups with more
than one.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-7-3
real_rings = ringed[.!occursin.(r"^[A-Za-z]+$", ringed.ring), :]
per_bird = combine(groupby(real_rings, [:ring, :species]), nrow => :n)
n_recaptured = count(>(1), per_bird.n)
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-7-3-check
check("7.3", n_recaptured)
```

About 4 500 birds contribute two records or more, one of them up to 43. Treating their
records as independent would overstate the sample size — and the colour codes would
have added 27 false "individuals" to the count.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-7-3
#| include: false
Checks.verify("7.3", n_recaptured)
```

## Distributions {#sec-eda-distributions}

Body mass across all birds spans three orders of magnitude, from hummingbirds to large
seabirds. On a linear scale almost everything piles up at the left; on a log scale the
shape becomes visible:

```{julia}
#| label: fig-mass-scales
#| fig-cap: "Body mass of all weighed birds, on a linear (a) and a logarithmic (b) scale."
masses = collect(skipmissing(birds.mass_g))

fig = Figure(size = (860, 340))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Body mass (g)", ylabel = "Records", title = "(a) Linear")
hist!(ax1, masses, bins = 60, color = (:steelblue, 0.7))
ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel = "Body mass (g, log scale)", title = "(b) Logarithmic",
           xscale = log10)
hist!(ax2, masses, bins = 10 .^ range(0, 3.6, length = 60), color = (:steelblue, 0.7))
fig
```

Sizes, areas and concentrations are bounded at zero and grow multiplicatively, so they
are usually right-skewed and closer to symmetric on a log scale. That is why models of
such variables so often use their logarithm.

Within one species the picture is different. For the white-necked thrush (*Turdus
albicollis*), one of the most recorded species, compare the distribution with a normal
curve of the same mean and standard deviation:

```{julia}
#| label: fig-thrush
#| fig-cap: "Body mass of *Turdus albicollis*: histogram with a normal curve of the same mean and standard deviation (a), and a QQ plot against the normal (b)."
thrush = collect(skipmissing(birds.mass_g[birds.species .== "Turdus albicollis"]))
μ, σ = mean(thrush), std(thrush)

fig = Figure(size = (860, 340))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Body mass (g)", ylabel = "Density", title = "(a) Histogram")
hist!(ax1, thrush, bins = 40, normalization = :pdf, color = (:seagreen, 0.6))
xs = range(minimum(thrush), maximum(thrush), length = 200)
lines!(ax1, xs, @.(exp(-(xs - μ)^2 / (2σ^2)) / (σ * sqrt(2π))), color = :black)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel = "Normal quantiles", ylabel = "Body mass (g)",
           title = "(b) QQ plot")
n = length(thrush)
z = quantile.(Normal(), ((1:n) .- 0.5) ./ n)
scatter!(ax2, z, sort(thrush), color = (:seagreen, 0.5), markersize = 5)
ablines!(ax2, μ, σ, color = :black, linestyle = :dash)
fig
```

Close to normal in the middle, with a few birds far lighter or heavier than the rest —
visible as the points that leave the line at both ends of the QQ plot. Those tails are
the subject of the next section.

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 7.4 — Mean or median?

Compute the median and the mean body mass of *Turdus albicollis* and pass them, in that
order, as a vector to `check("7.4", ...)`. Which is less affected by the extreme birds?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

`thrush` above already holds the masses. `[median(x), mean(x)]` builds the vector.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-7-4
thrush_centre = [median(thrush), mean(thrush)]
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-7-4-check
check("7.4", thrush_centre)
```

66 and 66.7 g: nearly equal, as expected for a roughly symmetric distribution. The
median ignores how extreme the tails are; the mean is pulled by them. With a few
records at 26 g or 114 g, the mean moves slightly; with the gross errors of the next
section, it would move much more.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-7-4
#| include: false
Checks.verify("7.4", thrush_centre)
```

## Errors and outliers {#sec-eda-outliers}

An overall histogram cannot show an error in a 14 g bird recorded as 1 240 g: 1 240 g
is a perfectly ordinary mass for a large bird. Outliers in trait data are outliers
**relative to the species**. A simple, robust flag compares each mass with the median
of its species:

```{julia}
#| label: mass-ratio
weighed = dropmissing(birds[:, [:species, :mass_g, :age, :status, :source]], :mass_g)
weighed = transform(groupby(weighed, :species),
                    :mass_g => median => :species_median, nrow => :n_species)
weighed.ratio = weighed.mass_g ./ weighed.species_median

suspicious = sort(weighed[(weighed.n_species .>= 10) .& (weighed.ratio .> 3), :],
                  :ratio, rev = true)
first(suspicious[:, [:species, :mass_g, :species_median, :ratio, :age, :status]], 8)
```

The top of the list shows several kinds of problem:

- *Thlypopsis sordida*, a 14 g tanager, recorded at more than 1 kg: almost certainly a
  data-entry error, perhaps a misplaced decimal separator or a wrong unit.
- Several masses about **ten times** the species median — 102 g for a 9 g flycatcher,
  50 g for a 4.5 g hummingbird: the signature of a shifted decimal point.
- Heavy juvenile *Tityra cayana* in a museum collection: possibly errors, possibly a
  mislabelled specimen. Only the source can tell.

Now the other tail:

```{julia}
#| label: mass-ratio-low
first(sort(weighed[(weighed.n_species .>= 10) .& (weighed.ratio .< 1/3), :], :ratio)[:,
      [:species, :mass_g, :species_median, :ratio, :age, :status]], 6)
```

Here some of the "outliers" are real. A 24 g slaty-breasted wood-rail (*Aramides
saracura*, median 346 g) marked as juvenile is plausibly a chick. Deleting it would
remove a real bird; keeping it in an analysis of adult size would distort it.

::: {.callout-important}
## Flag, don't delete

A statistical rule can only say that a value is unusual, never that it is wrong. Flag
suspicious values, look at them one by one, go back to the source where you can, and
decide — and write down what you decided and why, in code, so that the decision can be
reviewed. For many analyses the right choice is to restrict the data to what the
question is about (adults, say) rather than to remove individual points.
:::

The data also carry a quieter problem, **precision**. Most masses are whole numbers:

```{julia}
#| label: precision
mean(weighed.mass_g .== round.(weighed.mass_g))
```

72% of masses are integers, which means many were weighed to the nearest gram. For a
3 g hummingbird, rounding to the gram is an error of up to 17%; for a thrush, under 1%.
Precision that varies with the size of the animal is easy to miss and worth knowing
before you compare small species.

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 7.5 — How many suspicious masses?

Count the records whose mass is more than 3 times, or less than a third of, the median
of their species, among species with at least 10 weighed records. Pass the number to
`check("7.5", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

`weighed` already has `ratio` and `n_species`. Combine the conditions with `.&` and
`.|`, and count the `true`s with `count`.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-7-5
n_suspicious = count((weighed.n_species .>= 10) .&
                     ((weighed.ratio .> 3) .| (weighed.ratio .< 1/3)))
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-7-5-check
check("7.5", n_suspicious)
```

291 of about 60 000 weighed records, 0.5%: few, but enough to wreck a species mean.
The threshold of 3 is a choice, not a rule; with 2 you would flag more than twice as
many.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-7-5
#| include: false
Checks.verify("7.5", n_suspicious)
```

## Relationships and collinearity {#sec-eda-collinearity}

Morphological traits go together: big birds have long wings, long tails, long legs and
long bills. To see how strongly, summarize each species by the median of each trait —
the median, because of the outliers above — and compare species:

```{julia}
#| label: species-traits
traits = [:mass_g, :wing_mm, :tail_mm, :tarsus_mm, :bill_mm]
median_or_missing(x) = (v = collect(skipmissing(x)); isempty(v) ? missing : median(v))

by_species = dropmissing(combine(groupby(birds, :species),
                                 [t => median_or_missing => t for t in traits]...))
log_traits = DataFrame(log.(Matrix(by_species[:, traits])), traits)

nrow(by_species)
```

```{julia}
#| label: correlation-matrix
round.(cor(Matrix(log_traits)); digits = 2)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-pairs
#| fig-cap: "Species medians of five traits, on log scales, one point per species. Off the diagonal, each panel shows one pair of traits; on the diagonal, the distribution of each trait."
labels = ["log mass", "log wing", "log tail", "log tarsus", "log bill"]
fig = Figure(size = (820, 820))
for i in 1:5, j in 1:5
    ax = Axis(fig[i, j], xlabel = i == 5 ? labels[j] : "", ylabel = j == 1 ? labels[i] : "",
              xticklabelsvisible = i == 5, yticklabelsvisible = j == 1 && i != 1)
    if i == j                  # diagonal: the distribution of each trait (counts)
        hist!(ax, log_traits[:, i], bins = 25, color = (:grey60, 0.8))
    else
        scatter!(ax, log_traits[:, j], log_traits[:, i], markersize = 3,
                 color = (:steelblue, 0.5))
    end
end
fig
```

Mass and wing length are almost a single variable across species. If both entered a
model as predictors, the model could not tell their effects apart: the estimates would
be unstable and their standard errors large. The **variance inflation factor** measures
this. For each predictor, regress it on all the others; with $R^2$ from that
regression, $\text{VIF} = 1 / (1 - R^2)$:

```{julia}
#| label: vif
function vif(df, col)
    others = setdiff(propertynames(df), [col])
    f = Term(col) ~ sum(Term.(others))
    return 1 / (1 - r2(lm(f, df)))
end

DataFrame(trait = traits, vif = round.([vif(log_traits, t) for t in traits]; digits = 1))
```

@zuur2010protocol use a cut-off of 3; other authors use 5 or 10. Mass and wing length
are above all of them. The usual responses are
to keep only one of each collinear group, to combine them (a size index), or to ask a
question that does not need them separately.

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 7.6 — Mass and wing

What is the correlation between log body mass and log wing length across species, using
the species medians above? Pass it to `check("7.6", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

`cor(x, y)` on two columns of `log_traits`.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-7-6
r_mass_wing = cor(log_traits.mass_g, log_traits.wing_mm)
```

```{julia}
#| label: answer-7-6-check
check("7.6", r_mass_wing)
```

About 0.93. Across species, these two traits carry almost the same information.
Within a species it is much weaker — about 0.25 among individual *Turdus albicollis* —
because individuals of one species vary little in size: collinearity depends on the
scale of the question.
:::
:::

```{julia}
#| label: verify-7-6
#| include: false
Checks.verify("7.6", r_mass_wing)
```

## Why the plots: the Anscombe quartet {#sec-anscombe}

Summaries are not a substitute for looking. @anscombe1973graphs built four small data
sets with the same means, variances, correlations and regression lines:

```{julia}
#| label: anscombe-stats
anscombe = dataset("datasets", "anscombe")
DataFrame(set = 1:4,
          mean_x = [mean(anscombe[:, "X$i"]) for i in 1:4],
          mean_y = [round(mean(anscombe[:, "Y$i"]); digits = 2) for i in 1:4],
          cor_xy = [round(cor(anscombe[:, "X$i"], anscombe[:, "Y$i"]); digits = 3) for i in 1:4])
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-anscombe
#| fig-cap: "The Anscombe quartet: four data sets with the same summary statistics and the same least-squares line."
fig = Figure(size = (760, 560))
for i in 1:4
    x, y = anscombe[:, "X$i"], anscombe[:, "Y$i"]
    ax = Axis(fig[(i - 1) ÷ 2 + 1, (i - 1) % 2 + 1], title = "Set $i",
              limits = (3, 20, 3, 14))
    scatter!(ax, x, y, color = :steelblue)
    b = coef(lm(@formula(y ~ x), DataFrame(; x, y)))
    ablines!(ax, b[1], b[2], color = :darkorange)
end
fig
```

The first looks like what a linear model assumes. The second is a curve. In the third
one point pulls the line away from an otherwise perfect relationship. In the fourth the
whole slope depends on a single observation. Only the plots show it.

## Challenges {.unnumbered}

1. Plot the coordinates of all records (`lon`, `lat`) and colour them by
   `outside_range`. Are the records flagged as outside the species' range where you
   would expect? Are there points outside the Atlantic forest region altogether?
2. Male and female *Chiroxiphia caudata* (blue manakin) differ strikingly in plumage.
   Do they differ in mass? Compare the distributions, not only the medians, and decide
   what to do with records of `"Unknown"` sex.
3. Repeat the outlier rule of @sec-eda-outliers for wing length. Are the species with
   suspicious wings the same as those with suspicious masses? What would that tell you
   about the source of the errors?
